name: SH1107 FeatherWing OLED 128x64
description: 1.3" monochrome 128x64 OLED driven by a Sino Wealth SH1107 controller over I2C (400 kHz), 3 V logic and power, built-in DC-DC for the panel. The glass shows a 128-SEG by 64-COM window of the SH1107's 128x128 RAM starting at COM 0x60 (display offset 0x60), so SSD1306/SH1106 drivers do not work. Sold as: Adafruit FeatherWing OLED 128x64 (SH1107, product 4650), plugs onto a Feather (uses its 3V, GND, SDA, SCL) or wires through its STEMMA QT socket (GND, 3V, SDA, SCL); 2.2 k I2C pull-ups to 3V on board; I2C address 0x3C (0x3D with the ADDR jumper); also has buttons A/B/C and a reset button.
eli5: A small, very sharp black-and-white screen your board can write words and pictures on using just two wires.

pins.name: GND
pins.description: Ground (Feather GND; STEMMA QT pin 1, black)

pins.name: 3V
pins.description: Supply, 3.3 V only (Feather 3V; STEMMA QT pin 2, red). No regulator on the wing: never 5 V

pins.name: SDA
pins.description: I2C data (Feather SDA; STEMMA QT pin 3, blue), 2.2 k pull-up to 3V on board

pins.name: SCL
pins.description: I2C clock (Feather SCL; STEMMA QT pin 4, yellow), 2.2 k pull-up to 3V on board

buildNotes: Power from 3.3 V only: the wing has no regulator and the SH1107 logic/DC-DC supply is limited to 3.5 V.

The SH1107 is not an SSD1306: use the sh1107_featherwing driver (or Adafruit's SH1107 libraries). The board needs display offset 0x60 (D3h 60h), segment remap A0h, COM scan C0h and a 64-line multiplex (A8h 3Fh).
Page addressing: each of the 16 pages (B0h-BFh) holds 8 horizontal pixels; the column address picks the row, bottom row first, so the driver transposes its landscape framebuffer.
After display on (AFh) wait 100 ms before relying on the picture (datasheet power-on sequence).
Address 0x3C; close the ADDR jumper for 0x3D. The 2.2 k pull-ups are already on the wing.
Buttons A/B/C go to Feather pins (e.g. 9/6/5 on M0/M4, 15/32/14 on ESP32): only B has a pull-up, enable Pin.PULL_UP on the others.

RST (Feather header) is the Feather reset line, tied through closed jumper SJ1 to the OLED RES#; the wing already resets the OLED itself (APX803 supervisor plus 12 k pull-up), so it can stay unconnected with the 4-wire hookup. Adafruit's guide still suggests wiring RST to a non-Feather host's reset, which is harmless.

driver.code:
# MicroPython driver for the Adafruit FeatherWing OLED 128x64 (#4650), SH1107 over I2C.
# Init sequence and the glass wiring (display offset 0x60, segment remap A0, COM scan C0, 64-line multiplex)
# follow the Sino Wealth SH1107 datasheet v2.1 and Adafruit's own SH1107 drivers for this board.
# The drawing surface is a landscape 128x64 framebuf (x right, y down, buttons on the right edge).
#
# SH1107 RAM: page p (B0h-BFh) bits 0-7 drive SEG 8p..8p+7 (= landscape x); the column address
# (00h-0Fh / 10h-17h) is the line shown on a COM (= landscape row, the bottom row first on this board).
# A MONO_HMSB buffer holds 8 horizontal pixels per byte with bit 0 leftmost, so RAM byte (page p,
# column c) is simply buf[(63 - c) * 16 + p].
import framebuf
import time

_ADDR = 0x3C  # 0x3D with the ADDR jumper closed


class SH1107_FeatherWing(framebuf.FrameBuffer):
    def __init__(self, i2c, addr=_ADDR, contrast=0x4F):
        self.i2c = i2c
        self.addr = addr
        self.width = 128
        self.height = 64
        self.buf = bytearray(self.width * self.height // 8)
        super().__init__(self.buf, self.width, self.height, framebuf.MONO_HMSB)
        self._line = bytearray(65)
        self._line[0] = 0x40  # control byte: Co=0, D/C=1 -> display data follows
        self.init_display(contrast)

    def cmd(self, *bytes_):
        # control byte 0x00: Co=0, D/C=0 -> every following byte is a command
        self.i2c.writeto(self.addr, bytes((0x00,) + bytes_))

    def init_display(self, contrast=0x4F):
        self.cmd(0xAE)              # display off
        self.cmd(0xD5, 0x51)        # clock divide ratio / oscillator frequency
        self.cmd(0x20)              # page addressing mode (column auto-increments)
        self.cmd(0x81, contrast)    # contrast
        self.cmd(0xAD, 0x8A)        # built-in DC-DC on (turns on with the display)
        self.cmd(0xA0)              # segment remap off: data bit -> SEG as is
        self.cmd(0xC0)              # COM scan 0 -> N-1
        self.cmd(0xDC, 0x00)        # display start line 0
        self.cmd(0xD3, 0x60)        # display offset: the glass starts at COM 0x60 on this wing
        self.cmd(0xD9, 0x22)        # pre-charge / discharge period
        self.cmd(0xDB, 0x35)        # VCOM deselect level
        self.cmd(0xA8, 0x3F)        # multiplex ratio: 64 lines
        self.cmd(0xA4)              # show RAM contents
        self.cmd(0xA6)              # normal (not inverted)
        self.fill(0)
        self.show()                 # datasheet: clear the RAM before display on
        self.cmd(0xAF)              # display on
        time.sleep_ms(100)          # datasheet power-on sequence: wait 100 ms after AFh

    def poweroff(self):
        self.cmd(0xAE)

    def poweron(self):
        self.cmd(0xAF)
        time.sleep_ms(100)

    def contrast(self, value):
        self.cmd(0x81, value & 0xFF)

    def invert(self, on):
        self.cmd(0xA7 if on else 0xA6)

    def show(self):
        buf = self.buf
        line = self._line
        for p in range(16):
            self.cmd(0xB0 | p, 0x10, 0x00)  # page p, column 0
            i = 63 * 16 + p
            for c in range(64):
                line[c + 1] = buf[i]
                i -= 16
            self.i2c.writeto(self.addr, line)

example.code:
from machine import I2C, Pin
from sh1107_featherwing import SH1107_FeatherWing
i2c = I2C({I2C_ID}, sda=Pin({SDA}), scl=Pin({SCL}), freq=400000)
oled = SH1107_FeatherWing(i2c)
oled.fill(0)
oled.text('Sparkbench', 0, 0, 1)
oled.text('SH1107 OK', 0, 56, 1)
oled.show()
print('drawn')

test.title: Shows text on the top and bottom lines, upright

library.note: Passed the Sparkbench part check in simulation and matched an independent datasheet reading (1 difference(s) settled by a third reading with quoted evidence). Not yet tested on real hardware.
library.caveat: The picture's mounting orientation in simulation (sim.flip) comes from the vendor driver, not from a real panel; on real hardware the image may appear mirrored or rotated 180° and need the driver's rotate/flip option.
